newsitem.title: UK: No UK-style FDA seen by Labour.
newsitem.headline: No UK-style FDA seen by Labour.

text.p: The scientist charged by Labour leader Tony Blair with drawing up plans for a Food Standards Agency said on Friday he did not envisage a body along the lines of the powerful U.S. Food and Drug Administration.
Philip James, a professor at Scotland's Aberdeen University and an authority on food standards and nutrition, said he was more attracted by the Danish and Australian models than by the FDA.
"I would suspect that we need something rather different from the FDA," James, flanked by Blair, told reporters at the Scottish Labour party conference.

Blair told the conference he had asked James to begin work immediately on the remit of a food standards agency and to make recommendations on how it could be established as soon as possible after the election.
Labour is hot favourite to win the poll, which will probably be held on May 1.

Labour has become all the more determined to set up an agency to restore public confidence in food standards as a result of the failure, made known this week, of the ministry of agriculture to publicise a critical report on hygiene in abattoirs.

"After the events of the last few days, it is increasingly clear this is the right way to go but we can balance properly the interests of the industry and the interests of the consumer," Blair told reporters.

James said he would consult experts who have studied the Danish, Australian and U.S. models, but he noted that much of the work of the FDA is bound up with approving drugs, which requires it to have a large technical staff.

"And that of course would have very substantial implications in a UK context. We have a very different way of examining these issues, and what I have got to examine is whether we can get the best of the British system and add in the best of the American," the professor said.

He said the planned agency would have to be completely transparent, open and honest if public confidence is to be rebuilt after the crisis over mad cow disease and a recent outbreak of E.coli food poisoning.
"We'll get nowhere unless people have an absolute assurance that we're straight and that we're honest and that we admit when we don't know and indeed when we get it wrong," he said.
James said he envisaged that the new agency, though independent, would report to both the Ministry of Agriculture and the Department of Health.

"There are many examples of independent agencies that are being established or have already started working in other countries. I think we have to learn from their experience -- and that is the question of how you get independence and openness but accountability to parliament," he said.
